t: LeetCode 2162 — Minimum Cost to Set Cooking Time
o: The microwave reads whatever digits you push as four digits MMSS after prepending zeros: pushing 954 sets 09 minutes 54 seconds, and pushing 8090 means 80 minutes and 90 seconds (which add up to 81 min 30 s). Each press costs pushCost, moving the finger between different digits costs moveCost, and the finger starts on startAt. Several digit strings realize the same targetSeconds — 600 seconds can be typed as 1000, 960, or 0960, costing 12 versus 12 versus 9 in Example 1 — so choosing the string matters as much as choosing the decomposition. Example 2 shows 76 beats 076 and 116 for a target of 76 seconds because shorter strings mean fewer presses. Since targetSeconds <= 6039 = 99*60 + 99, only decompositions with both parts in 0..99 matter.
k: A setting is valid iff minutes m and seconds s satisfy 60m + s = targetSeconds with 0 <= m, s <= 99; the typed string is str(m) (dropped when m = 0) followed by s zero-padded to two digits.
Only two decompositions can exist — (m, s) and the borrowed (m-1, s+60) — because s + 120 would violate the 99-second cap.
Never type unnecessary leading zeros: each extra press costs pushCost and possibly moveCost.

a.i: Enumerate every minute count m from 0 to 99, derive s = targetSeconds - 60*m, and keep pairs with 0 <= s <= 99. Format each survivor exactly as the microwave normalizes it, simulate the finger, and take the cheapest. At most 100 candidates makes correctness obvious and runtime trivial.
s: For m in 0..99 compute s = targetSeconds - 60*m; skip unless 0 <= s <= 99.
Build the digit string: decimal m (omitted when 0) plus s padded to two digits.
Simulate typing from startAt: add moveCost on each digit change, pushCost per press.
Return the minimum cost over all candidates.
a.t: O(1) — at most 100 candidate decompositions, each typed in at most 4 presses

a.n: Approach 2: Reduce to at most two candidates (optimal)
a.i: Seconds cannot exceed 99, so the natural remainder s = targetSeconds % 60 absorbs at most one borrowed minute. The only possible decompositions are (m, s) — valid when m <= 99 — and (m-1, s+60), valid when m >= 1 and s <= 39. Comparing the typing cost of just these two digit strings solves everything in constant time.
s: Split m = targetSeconds / 60 and s = targetSeconds % 60.
Candidate A: (m, s), admissible when m <= 99.
Candidate B: (m-1, s+60), admissible when m >= 1 and s <= 39.
Evaluate the typing cost of both strings and return the cheaper.
a.t: O(1) — at most two candidates, each evaluated over at most 4 digits

w: Say the key sentence early — only two decompositions exist — and the rest is a formatting exercise. Pitfalls: emitting a leading zero for minutes (typing 076 wastes presses versus 76), omitting the zero-padding of seconds ('06' must be typed for 6 seconds), dropping the m >= 1 guard on the borrowed candidate, and forgetting that targetSeconds >= 6000 makes the direct candidate illegal since its minute part is 100. Follow-ups: per-digit push costs, a keypad where move cost is Manhattan distance, or returning all minimal-cost typings.
